examples.question: What is national income?
examples.answer: National income is the total money value of all goods and services produced by a country within a given period, usually one year. It measures the economic performance of a nation. It can be looked at in three ways that should give the same total: the output (product) approach, the income approach, and the expenditure approach. Key related terms include Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Gross National Product (GNP) and Net National Product (NNP). WAEC frequently tests the meaning and methods of measuring national income.

examples.question: Differentiate between GDP and GNP.
examples.answer: GDP (Gross Domestic Product) is the total value of all goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year, regardless of who produces them (citizens or foreigners). GNP (Gross National Product) is the total value of goods and services produced by a country's citizens in a year, whether at home or abroad. The link is: GNP = GDP + net income from abroad (income earned by citizens abroad minus income earned by foreigners within the country). So GDP is about location, while GNP is about ownership/nationality.

examples.question: Why is national income used to measure standard of living?
examples.answer: National income, especially per capita income (national income divided by population), is used to estimate the average standard of living, because a higher income per person usually means people can afford more goods and services. However, it is not a perfect measure for several reasons: (1) it ignores how income is distributed, so a few rich people can raise the average while many remain poor; (2) it does not show the kinds of goods produced (more weapons does not improve welfare); and (3) it ignores leisure, environmental damage and the informal sector. So national income should be used alongside other indicators when judging welfare.

examples.question: How should I answer comprehension questions to score high marks?
examples.answer:
Follow this method every time.

Step 1: read the passage once quickly to get the general idea.
Step 2: read the QUESTIONS next, so you know what to look for.
Step 3: read the passage again slowly, underlining the parts that answer each question.
Step 4: answer in COMPLETE SENTENCES, in your own words where possible — copying whole chunks blindly rarely earns full marks.
Step 5: match your answer's length to the marks: one mark needs one point, three marks need three points.
Step 6: never bring in outside knowledge or opinions; every answer must come from the passage itself. Finally, watch the question word: 'state' wants a fact, 'explain' wants reasons, 'according to the passage' means the author's view, not yours. Leave no question blank — an attempted answer may earn something.

examples.question: How do I work out the meaning of a word I don't know in a passage?
examples.answer:
Use CONTEXT CLUES — the surrounding words that hint at the meaning. Four clue types to look for.

DEFINITION: the passage explains it directly, as in 'The drought, a long period without rain, destroyed the crops.'
CONTRAST: a word like but, although or unlike signals the opposite, as in 'Unlike his talkative brother, Musa was taciturn' — so taciturn means quiet.
EXAMPLE: 'Tubers such as yam, cassava and cocoyam grow underground' tells you what tubers are.
GENERAL SENSE: read the whole sentence and ask what word would fit, as in 'After trekking for hours under the hot sun, the farmer was famished and ate two plates of food' — famished must mean very hungry. Also break the word into parts: 'unhappy' is un- (not) plus happy. Guess from clues first, then confirm with a dictionary later.

examples.question: What is a paragraph and how do I write a good one?
examples.answer: A paragraph is a group of sentences that develop ONE main idea. A good paragraph has three parts. The TOPIC SENTENCE states the main idea, usually first: 'Our school compound is very clean.' The SUPPORTING SENTENCES explain, give reasons or examples: 'Every morning, pupils sweep their assigned areas. The refuse bins are emptied daily, and flowers line the pathways.' The CONCLUDING SENTENCE rounds it off or links to the next idea: 'Visitors often praise how neat the environment looks.' Rules to follow: indent or leave a line at the start; keep to one idea per paragraph and start a new one when the idea changes; and aim for four to six sentences. A composition with no paragraphs is hard to read and loses organisation marks, no matter how good the content.

examples.question: How do I write a good narrative composition?
examples.answer:
A narrative tells a story, so it needs a clear structure.

INTRODUCTION: set the scene — who, where and when: 'It was the last day of the second term when our class went on an excursion to Olumo Rock.'
BODY: narrate events in the ORDER they happened, using time expressions like first, then, after that, suddenly and finally. Build towards the most exciting moment (the climax).
CONCLUSION: say how it ended and what you felt or learnt: 'We returned home tired but happy, and I will never forget that day.' Key tips: write mostly in the PAST tense and keep it consistent; use vivid details and the five senses; include a little direct speech to bring it alive; and stay strictly on the given topic. Plan for five minutes before writing — a jotted outline of your events prevents a rambling story.

examples.question: What layout and parts does an informal letter need in a JSS1 exam?
examples.answer:
An informal (friendly) letter goes to someone you know well — a friend or relative — and has five parts.

First, YOUR ADDRESS at the top right-hand corner, written line by line.
Second, the DATE directly under the address: '15th July, 2026.'
Third, the SALUTATION on the left: 'Dear Ada,' — always with a comma.
Fourth, the BODY in paragraphs: begin by asking after the person's wellbeing, then give your news or message, then close warmly.
Fifth, the SUBSCRIPT (closing): 'Your loving friend,' or 'Yours sincerely,' followed by your first name only.

Remember: an informal letter carries ONLY your own address, never the receiver's, and it has no heading or title. Keep the language warm and conversational — contractions like 'I'm' and 'don't' are perfectly acceptable here, unlike in a formal letter.

examples.question: What is the difference between a formal and an informal letter?
examples.answer:
They differ in audience, format and language.

AUDIENCE: an informal letter goes to friends and family; a formal letter goes to officials — your principal, an employer, a newspaper editor.
ADDRESSES: informal letters carry only your address; formal letters carry your address AND the receiver's address on the left.
HEADING: formal letters need a title stating the purpose, such as 'APPLICATION FOR A PLACE IN YOUR SCHOOL', usually underlined; informal letters have none.
SALUTATION AND CLOSING: informal uses 'Dear Chidi,' with 'Your loving friend,'; formal uses 'Dear Sir/Madam,' with 'Yours faithfully,' (or 'Yours sincerely,' when you know the name).
LANGUAGE: informal allows contractions and chatty expressions; formal requires full words, polite and serious tone, and no slang. Choosing the wrong register is a common and costly exam error.

examples.question: How can I improve my vocabulary?
examples.answer:
Vocabulary grows through deliberate daily habits.

First, READ widely — newspapers, storybooks and your textbooks — because reading exposes you to words in natural use.
Second, keep a VOCABULARY NOTEBOOK: write each new word, its meaning, and your OWN sentence using it; a word is only truly yours once you have used it.
Third, learn words in FAMILIES: from 'happy' you get happiness, unhappy, happily.
Fourth, study synonyms and antonyms so you can vary your writing instead of repeating 'good' and 'nice'.
Fifth, learn common prefixes and suffixes: un- and dis- mean not, re- means again, -ful means full of.
Sixth, USE new words when speaking and writing — five new words a week becomes over 250 a year.
Finally, always confirm meanings in a dictionary before using a word in an exam.

examples.question: How do I find the main idea of a passage?
examples.answer:
The main idea is what the whole passage is mostly about — not a small detail from one line. Use these steps.

Step 1: check the TITLE if there is one, as it often states the subject directly.
Step 2: read the FIRST and LAST paragraphs carefully; writers usually introduce the main idea early and restate it at the end.
Step 3: find the TOPIC SENTENCE of each paragraph and see what they have in common.
Step 4: ask yourself, 'If I had to tell a friend in one sentence what this passage is about, what would I say?' That sentence is the main idea.
Step 5: test your answer — the main idea must cover the WHOLE passage. If your statement only fits one paragraph, it is a supporting detail, not the main idea. Watch for repeated words, since writers repeat what matters most.

examples.question: What is a noun?
examples.answer: A noun is a word that names a person, place, animal or thing. For example: 'Emeka' names a person, 'Lagos' names a place, 'goat' names an animal, and 'pencil' names a thing. Nouns can also name ideas we cannot touch, like 'happiness' or 'honesty'. A quick test: if you can put 'the' or 'a' in front of a word and it makes sense (the market, a teacher), it is usually a noun.

examples.question: Identify the verb in this sentence: Amina sells akara every morning.
examples.answer: Let us find the verb. A verb is an action word, or a word that tells what someone or something does. In 'Amina sells akara every morning', ask: what does Amina do? She sells. So the verb is 'sells'. 'Amina' is a noun (the doer), 'akara' is a noun (what is sold), and 'every morning' tells us when. The action word, the verb, is 'sells'.

examples.question: Why do we use adjectives?
examples.answer: Good question! We use adjectives to describe nouns, that is, to tell us more about a person, place, animal or thing. Without adjectives, sentences would be plain. Compare: 'I bought a bag' with 'I bought a big, red bag.' The words 'big' and 'red' are adjectives, and they help the listener picture exactly what you mean. So adjectives make our speaking and writing clearer and more interesting.

examples.question: Pick out the pronoun: Chidi said he would travel to Abuja.
examples.answer: A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun so we do not repeat the noun again and again. In 'Chidi said he would travel to Abuja', instead of saying 'Chidi said Chidi would travel', we replace the second 'Chidi' with 'he'. So the pronoun is 'he'. Other common pronouns are I, you, she, it, we and they.

examples.question: What are the eight parts of speech?
examples.answer: Every English word belongs to one of eight parts of speech, according to the job it does in a sentence. NOUN — names a person, place, thing or idea: Emeka, Lagos, book, freedom. PRONOUN — replaces a noun: he, she, it, they, we. VERB — shows action or state of being: run, eat, is, become. ADJECTIVE — describes a noun: tall, red, delicious. ADVERB — describes a verb, adjective or another adverb, often telling how, when or where: quickly, yesterday, very. PREPOSITION — shows a relationship of position or time: on, under, before, between. CONJUNCTION — joins words or sentences: and, but, because, although. INTERJECTION — expresses sudden feeling: Wow! Oh! Alas! Remember: a word's part of speech depends on its JOB in that particular sentence, not on the word alone.

examples.question: What are the types of nouns?
examples.answer: Nouns are grouped into five main types. COMMON nouns name things in general and take a small letter: boy, city, river. PROPER nouns name particular people, places or things and always take a capital letter: Amina, Kano, River Niger, Monday. ABSTRACT nouns name things you cannot touch — ideas, feelings and qualities: love, honesty, freedom, poverty. COLLECTIVE nouns name a group taken as one unit: a flock of birds, a herd of cattle, a bunch of bananas, a team of players. CONCRETE nouns name things you can perceive with your senses: table, water, drum. Nouns are also countable (book/books, which you can count) or uncountable (rice, sand, water, which you measure instead). Getting the capital letter right on proper nouns is a frequent exam mark.

examples.question: What is an adverb and how is it different from an adjective?
examples.answer: An ADJECTIVE describes a NOUN, while an ADVERB describes a VERB, an adjective or another adverb. Compare these two sentences: 'Ngozi is a quick runner' — quick describes the noun 'runner', so it is an adjective. 'Ngozi runs quickly' — quickly describes the verb 'runs', so it is an adverb. Adverbs answer the questions HOW (quickly, carefully, well), WHEN (yesterday, soon, always), WHERE (here, outside, everywhere) and HOW OFTEN (rarely, twice, daily). Many adverbs are formed by adding -ly to an adjective: careful becomes carefully, happy becomes happily. But beware of exceptions: 'fast' and 'hard' stay the same, and 'good' becomes 'well'. So we say 'She sings well', never 'She sings good'.

examples.question: What is a preposition? Give examples in sentences.
examples.answer: A preposition is a word that shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and another word in the sentence — usually a relationship of position, direction or time. Common ones: in, on, at, under, over, between, beside, from, to, before, after, with. In sentences: 'The book is ON the table' (position). 'Amina travelled TO Ibadan' (direction). 'We resume AFTER the holiday' (time). 'The ball rolled UNDER the chair' (position). 'He shared the mangoes BETWEEN his two sisters' (relationship). A helpful trick: many prepositions describe where a lizard can go relative to a wall — on it, under it, over it, beside it, behind it, near it. Note the fixed Nigerian-exam favourites: we say 'good AT mathematics', 'married TO someone', and 'congratulate someone ON success'.

examples.question: What are conjunctions and how do I use them?
examples.answer: A conjunction is a joining word — it links words, phrases or whole sentences. COORDINATING conjunctions join items of equal weight: and, but, or, so, yet, for, nor. Examples: 'Bola AND Tunde came to school.' 'I was tired, BUT I finished my homework.' 'Will you take rice OR beans?' SUBORDINATING conjunctions join a main idea to a dependent one, often showing reason, time or condition: because, although, when, while, if, since, unless, until. Examples: 'We stayed indoors BECAUSE it was raining.' 'ALTHOUGH he was tired, he read his book.' 'Call me WHEN you arrive.' Conjunctions turn short choppy sentences into flowing ones, which examiners reward in composition — instead of 'It rained. We stayed inside.' write 'We stayed inside because it rained.'

examples.question: Identify the part of speech of each word in: The clever girl quickly answered.
examples.answer: Let us take the sentence word by word, asking what job each word does. THE — an article (a special kind of determiner, sometimes classed with adjectives) pointing to a particular girl. CLEVER — an adjective, because it describes the noun 'girl'. GIRL — a noun, naming a person; it is the subject of the sentence. QUICKLY — an adverb, because it describes HOW the action was done, and notice the -ly ending. ANSWERED — a verb, the action word, in the past tense. So the pattern is: article, adjective, noun, adverb, verb. The method to use every time: find the verb (the action) first, then ask who or what did it (the noun or pronoun subject), then check what the remaining words describe.

examples.question: Can the same word be different parts of speech?
examples.answer: Yes — and this is why you must always look at the word's JOB in the sentence, never memorise words as belonging to one class. Take the word 'water'. In 'The WATER is cold', it names a thing, so it is a noun. In 'Please WATER the flowers', it is an action, so it is a verb. Take 'well'. In 'She sings WELL', it describes the verb, so it is an adverb. In 'They drew water from the WELL', it names a thing, so it is a noun. Another: in 'Book a seat' book is a verb, while in 'Read the book' it is a noun. So when an exam asks for the part of speech of an underlined word, read the whole sentence and ask: what work is this word doing HERE?

examples.question: What are the types of pronouns?
examples.answer: Pronouns replace nouns so we do not repeat them awkwardly. PERSONAL pronouns stand for people or things: I, you, he, she, it, we, they (as subjects) and me, him, her, us, them (as objects). POSSESSIVE pronouns show ownership: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. REFLEXIVE pronouns point back to the subject: myself, yourself, himself, herself, ourselves, themselves — as in 'She cooked the rice herself.' DEMONSTRATIVE pronouns point out: this, that, these, those. INTERROGATIVE pronouns ask questions: who, whom, whose, which, what. RELATIVE pronouns join clauses: who, whom, whose, which, that — as in 'The boy WHO won the prize is my friend.' Without pronouns we would write 'Emeka took Emeka's book because Emeka needed Emeka's book' instead of the natural version.

examples.question: What is a sentence and what are its main parts?
examples.answer: A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought. It must begin with a capital letter and end with a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark. Every complete sentence has two main parts. The SUBJECT is who or what the sentence is about — usually a noun or pronoun. The PREDICATE says something about the subject and always contains the verb. In 'Amina reads her book every evening', the subject is 'Amina' and the predicate is 'reads her book every evening'. A group of words missing either part, like 'Running down the street', is not a sentence but a FRAGMENT, because it leaves the thought incomplete — we do not know who was running. To test any group of words, ask: who or what? and what did they do?

examples.question: What are the four types of sentences by purpose?
examples.answer: Sentences are classified by what they do. A DECLARATIVE sentence makes a statement and ends with a full stop: 'Abuja is the capital of Nigeria.' An INTERROGATIVE sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark: 'What time does school close?' An IMPERATIVE sentence gives a command or makes a request, and the subject 'you' is usually understood rather than written: 'Close the door.' 'Please pass me the chalk.' An EXCLAMATORY sentence expresses strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark: 'What a beautiful day!' 'How well she sang!' Matching the right punctuation to each type is where marks are won or lost, so check every sentence you write: is it telling, asking, commanding or exclaiming?

examples.question: What is the difference between a simple, compound and complex sentence?
examples.answer: The difference lies in how many clauses the sentence contains. A SIMPLE sentence has one main clause — one subject and one verb expressing a complete thought: 'Chidi plays football.' A COMPOUND sentence joins two or more main clauses, each able to stand alone, using a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, so): 'Chidi plays football, AND his sister plays volleyball.' Remove either half and it still makes sense. A COMPLEX sentence joins a main clause to a subordinate clause that cannot stand alone, using a subordinating conjunction (because, although, when, if): 'Chidi plays football BECAUSE he wants to be fit.' The part 'because he wants to be fit' is incomplete by itself. Good compositions mix all three — using only simple sentences makes writing sound childish.

examples.question: What is subject-verb agreement?
examples.answer: Subject-verb agreement (concord) means the verb must match its subject in number. A SINGULAR subject takes a singular verb, and a PLURAL subject takes a plural verb. Correct: 'The boy RUNS fast' (singular) and 'The boys RUN fast' (plural). Notice the -s pattern is opposite to nouns: the -s goes on the singular VERB but on the plural NOUN. Watch these traps. Words between subject and verb do not change the agreement: 'The basket of oranges IS heavy' — the subject is 'basket', not 'oranges'. Subjects joined by 'and' are plural: 'Bola and Musa ARE here.' But 'each', 'every', 'everyone' and 'nobody' are singular: 'Everyone IS present.' Reading your sentence aloud, stripping away the extra words, usually reveals the right verb.

examples.question: Correct this sentence: The pupils in my class is very hardworking.
examples.answer:
The correct sentence is: 'The pupils in my class ARE very hardworking.' Here is the reasoning.

Step 1: find the true subject. It is 'pupils', which is plural — 'in my class' is only a prepositional phrase adding information.
Step 2: match the verb to that subject. Plural subject 'pupils' needs the plural verb 'are', not the singular 'is'. The phrase 'in my class' misleads students because 'class' sits right next to the verb and sounds singular. Strip out the phrase and the error becomes obvious: 'The pupils IS hardworking' is clearly wrong.

Always locate the head noun of the subject before choosing the verb. More practice: 'The bag of books IS heavy' (bag, singular) but 'The books in the bag ARE heavy' (books, plural).

examples.question: Why is punctuation important? Give the main marks and their uses.
examples.answer: Punctuation guides the reader and can completely change meaning — compare 'Let us eat, Grandma' with 'Let us eat Grandma'! The main marks: FULL STOP (.) ends a statement. QUESTION MARK (?) ends a question. EXCLAMATION MARK (!) shows strong feeling. COMMA (,) marks a short pause, separates items in a list ('We bought yam, rice, beans and oil') and follows an introductory phrase. APOSTROPHE (') shows possession ('Ade's book') or contraction ('don't'). QUOTATION MARKS (" ") enclose direct speech: 'The teacher said, "Open your books."' COLON (:) introduces a list or explanation. SEMICOLON (;) links two closely related sentences. CAPITAL LETTERS begin sentences and proper nouns. Careless punctuation costs easy marks in every English paper.

examples.question: How do I change a statement into a question?
examples.answer: There are two main ways. FIRST, with a helping verb already present, simply move it in front of the subject. 'She IS reading' becomes 'IS she reading?' 'They CAN swim' becomes 'CAN they swim?' SECOND, when there is no helping verb, borrow do, does or did, and return the main verb to its base form. 'Musa plays football' becomes 'DOES Musa PLAY football?' — note 'plays' loses its -s. 'They went home' becomes 'DID they GO home?' — note 'went' returns to 'go'. You can also use question words at the front for specific information: What, Where, When, Why, Who, Which and How, as in 'WHERE does Musa play football?' Every question ends with a question mark — forgetting it is a needless lost mark.

examples.question: What is the difference between direct and indirect speech?
examples.answer:
DIRECT speech reports the speaker's exact words inside quotation marks: The teacher said, "I am marking your books." INDIRECT (reported) speech tells what was said without quoting exactly: The teacher said that she was marking our books. Three things usually change when you convert.

First, quotation marks disappear and 'that' is often added.
Second, the tense normally shifts back one step: 'am' becomes 'was', 'will' becomes 'would', 'can' becomes 'could'.
Third, pronouns and time words adjust to the new speaker's viewpoint: 'I' may become 'she', 'your' becomes 'our', 'today' becomes 'that day', and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'. Example: Ada said, "I will travel tomorrow" becomes Ada said that she would travel the next day.

examples.question: What are the three main tenses in English?
examples.answer: Tense shows the TIME of an action, and there are three main ones. PRESENT tense describes what happens now or habitually: 'Ada writes a letter.' 'The sun rises in the east.' PAST tense describes what already happened: 'Ada wrote a letter yesterday.' FUTURE tense describes what has not yet happened: 'Ada will write a letter tomorrow.' Each of these has forms that add more detail — for example the present continuous ('Ada is writing') for an action happening at this moment, and the present perfect ('Ada has written') for an action just completed. Time expressions are your clue to the required tense: now, every day and always signal present; yesterday, last week and ago signal past; tomorrow, next month and soon signal future.

examples.question: What is the difference between simple present and present continuous?
examples.answer: The SIMPLE PRESENT describes habits, routines and general truths — things that happen regularly rather than right now: 'I eat rice every Sunday.' 'Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.' 'She teaches at our school.' The PRESENT CONTINUOUS describes an action happening at this very moment, and is formed with is/am/are plus a verb ending in -ing: 'I am eating rice now.' 'She is teaching in the next classroom.' Compare carefully: 'Musa plays football' means he plays regularly, perhaps for the school team; 'Musa is playing football' means he is on the pitch at this moment. Time words help you choose: every day, always, usually and often go with simple present, while now, at the moment and look! go with present continuous.

examples.question: How do I form the past tense of regular and irregular verbs?
examples.answer: REGULAR verbs form the past tense by adding -ed: walk becomes walked, play becomes played, jump becomes jumped. Note the spelling rules: verbs ending in -e just add -d (love becomes loved); verbs ending in a consonant plus -y change y to i and add -ed (study becomes studied, carry becomes carried); and short verbs ending in a single consonant double it (stop becomes stopped, plan becomes planned). IRREGULAR verbs change form completely and must be memorised: go becomes went, eat becomes ate, see becomes saw, take becomes took, write becomes wrote, buy becomes bought, bring becomes brought, teach becomes taught, catch becomes caught. There is no rule for these — the best method is to use five of them in your own sentences each day until they stick.

examples.question: What is the present perfect tense and when do I use it?
examples.answer:
The present perfect is formed with HAS or HAVE plus the past participle: 'She HAS eaten.' 'They HAVE travelled.' Use 'has' with he, she and it, and 'have' with I, you, we and they. You use it in three situations.

First, for an action completed recently, with the result still relevant: 'I have finished my homework' (so it is ready now).
Second, for an action at an unspecified time in the past: 'I have visited Kano before' — we are not saying when.
Third, for something that started in the past and continues: 'She has lived in Enugu for ten years.' Key contrast: 'I ate rice' (simple past) needs a finished time like yesterday, while 'I have eaten rice' focuses on the present result — you are not hungry now. Words like already, just, ever, never, since and for often signal it.

examples.question: Correct this sentence: Yesterday, Bola go to the market and buy tomatoes.
examples.answer:
The correct sentence is: 'Yesterday, Bola WENT to the market and BOUGHT tomatoes.' Here is the reasoning.

Step 1: spot the time word 'Yesterday', which tells us the action is finished, so every verb must be in the past tense.
Step 2: correct each verb. 'Go' is irregular, and its past tense is 'went', not 'goed'. 'Buy' is also irregular, and its past tense is 'bought', not 'buyed'.
Step 3: check consistency — both verbs describe the same past trip, so both must be past; mixing 'went' with 'buy' would be inconsistent. This kind of error is very common in speech, but in writing the examiner expects full agreement between the time word and every verb in the sentence.

examples.question: What are the different ways of expressing future time in English?
examples.answer:
There are three common ways.

First, WILL plus the base verb, for decisions, promises and predictions: 'I will call you tonight.' 'It will rain tomorrow.'
Second, GOING TO plus the base verb, for plans already made or things you can see coming: 'We are going to visit our grandmother next week.' 'Look at those dark clouds — it is going to rain.'
Third, the PRESENT CONTINUOUS for fixed arrangements with a set time: 'I am travelling to Onitsha on Friday.' The simple present can even carry future meaning for timetabled events: 'The bus leaves at 6 a.m. tomorrow.' Note that after 'will', the verb never changes form — say 'She will come', never 'She will comes' or 'She will came'.

examples.question: Change this sentence to the past continuous tense: The children play in the field.
examples.answer: The past continuous becomes: 'The children WERE PLAYING in the field.' Here is how it is formed: WAS or WERE plus a verb ending in -ing. Use 'was' with singular subjects (I, he, she, it) and 'were' with plural subjects (you, we, they). Since 'children' is plural, we use 'were', and 'play' becomes 'playing'. What does this tense mean? It describes an action that was ongoing at some point in the past, often interrupted by another action: 'The children were playing in the field WHEN the rain started.' Compare the three: 'The children play' (habit), 'The children played' (finished action), 'The children were playing' (action in progress at that past moment). The continuous form paints a picture of the action still happening.

examples.question: Why do we say 'He goes' but 'They go'?
examples.answer: This is the third-person singular rule of the simple present tense. When the subject is he, she, it, or any singular noun, the verb takes -s or -es. When the subject is I, you, we, they, or any plural noun, the verb stays in its base form. So: 'He GOES to school' but 'They GO to school'; 'She WRITES neatly' but 'We WRITE neatly'; 'The boy PLAYS' but 'The boys PLAY'. Spelling notes: add -es to verbs ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x or -o (goes, watches, washes, fixes), and change y to ies after a consonant (study becomes studies). Remember the reversal that confuses many students: for NOUNS the -s means plural, but for VERBS the -s means singular. 'The boys play' has the s on the noun; 'The boy plays' has it on the verb.

examples.question: What is the difference between active and passive voice?
examples.answer: Voice tells us whether the subject of a sentence is doing the action or receiving it. In the ACTIVE voice, the subject does the action: 'Ngozi cooked the rice.' Here Ngozi (the doer) comes first and performs the cooking. In the PASSIVE voice, the subject receives the action: 'The rice was cooked by Ngozi.' Now 'the rice' (the receiver) comes first, and the doer moves to the end after 'by'. The active voice is direct and lively, so we use it most of the time. The passive is useful when the doer is unknown or unimportant, as in 'My bag was stolen' — we may not know who did it. Both are correct; you choose based on what you want to emphasise.

examples.question: How do I change an active sentence to passive? Use 'The teacher punished the boy.'
examples.answer:
Let us change 'The teacher punished the boy' to the passive voice, step by step.

Step 1: find the object of the active sentence — 'the boy' — and move it to the front to become the new subject.
Step 2: change the verb using the correct form of 'to be' plus the past participle. 'Punished' becomes 'was punished'.
Step 3: move the original subject, 'the teacher', to the end and put 'by' before it. Putting it together: 'The boy was punished by the teacher.'

So the three moves are: object to the front, verb becomes 'be' + past participle, and the doer goes to the back with 'by'. Follow this order every time and the change is easy.

examples.question: Change to passive: Amina is writing a letter.
examples.answer:
Let us convert 'Amina is writing a letter' to the passive voice.

Step 1: the object 'a letter' moves to the front as the new subject.
Step 2: keep the tense the same. The sentence is in the present continuous ('is writing'), so the passive must also be continuous: use 'is being' plus the past participle 'written'.
Step 3: move 'Amina' to the end with 'by'. The result is: 'A letter is being written by Amina.' The important lesson here is that the tense never changes when you switch voice; only the arrangement and the verb form change. Present continuous stays present continuous, past stays past, and so on.

Always check that your passive keeps the original tense.

examples.question: Change to active: The song was sung by the choir.
examples.answer:
Let us turn the passive sentence 'The song was sung by the choir' back into the active voice.

Step 1: find the doer, which comes after 'by' — here it is 'the choir'. Move it to the front to become the subject.
Step 2: change the verb from the passive 'was sung' to the simple active past 'sang', keeping the same past tense.
Step 3: the old subject 'the song' becomes the object and moves after the verb. The active sentence is: 'The choir sang the song.'

Notice the active version is shorter and more direct. Going from passive to active is simply the reverse of the earlier steps: the doer leads, and the receiver follows the verb.

examples.question: When should I use the passive voice?
examples.answer:
The passive voice is useful in four main situations.

First, when the doer is unknown: 'My phone was stolen at the park' — we do not know the thief.
Second, when the doer is obvious or unimportant: 'The results will be released next week' — everyone knows the school does it.
Third, when we want to be tactful and avoid blaming a person: 'A mistake was made' sounds gentler than naming who erred.
Fourth, in formal and scientific writing: 'The water was heated to 100 degrees.' In everyday speech and most compositions, though, prefer the active voice because it is clearer and livelier. Use the passive deliberately, for these reasons, rather than by accident.

examples.question: What is a past participle and why does the passive need it?
examples.answer: The past participle is the third form of a verb, the one often used after 'have' or 'be'. For regular verbs it ends in -ed, the same as the past tense: play, played, played. For irregular verbs it is different and must be learnt: eat, ate, eaten; write, wrote, written; sing, sang, sung; take, took, taken; break, broke, broken. The passive voice always uses a form of 'be' plus this past participle, as in 'is eaten', 'was written', 'will be taken'. That is why knowing your participles matters: if you say 'The letter was wrote', it is wrong; the past participle 'written' is needed, giving 'The letter was written'. Learn the three forms of common irregular verbs and the passive becomes easy.

examples.question: Change to passive: They will build a new school in our village.
examples.answer:
Let us change 'They will build a new school in our village' to the passive voice.

Step 1: the object 'a new school' moves to the front as the new subject.
Step 2: the sentence is in the future tense ('will build'), so the passive uses 'will be' plus the past participle 'built'.
Step 3: the doer 'they' is vague and unimportant, so we can drop it or keep 'by them'. The natural passive is: 'A new school will be built in our village.' Here the passive actually reads better, because who builds it does not matter — the school is the point. The extra detail 'in our village' simply stays where it was. Future active becomes future passive: 'will' plus 'be' plus participle.

examples.question: Can every sentence be changed to passive?
examples.answer: No, only sentences with a transitive verb — a verb that has an object — can be made passive, because the passive works by moving the object to the front. 'Emeka kicked the ball' has the object 'the ball', so it becomes 'The ball was kicked by Emeka.' But 'Emeka slept' has no object; 'sleep' is an intransitive verb, so it cannot be made passive. The same goes for verbs like go, come, arrive, laugh and die. A quick test: ask 'the verb what?' If there is an answer (kicked WHAT? the ball), the sentence has an object and can go passive. If there is no answer, it cannot. So always check for an object before trying to change a sentence to the passive voice.

examples.question: What does concord (subject-verb agreement) mean, and why does it matter for BECE?
examples.answer: Concord, also called agreement, means matching words correctly so a sentence sounds right. The most important type is subject-verb concord: the verb must agree with its subject in number. A singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. For example, 'The boy runs' is singular, while 'The boys run' is plural. Notice the -s pattern is the opposite of nouns: it goes on the singular verb but the plural noun. Concord is one of the most tested areas in BECE and WAEC because errors are so common in everyday speech. Master it and you will write and speak far more correctly.

examples.question: Choose the correct verb: The list of names (is/are) on the table.
examples.answer:
The correct answer is 'is': 'The list of names is on the table.' Here is the reasoning.

Step 1: find the true subject of the sentence. It is 'the list', which is singular.
Step 2: ignore the words in between. 'Of names' is only a prepositional phrase describing the list; it does not change the subject.
Step 3: match the verb to the real subject, so singular 'list' takes singular 'is'. The plural noun 'names' sitting right before the verb is a trap examiners love. Whenever a phrase separates the subject from the verb, mentally remove it and the correct verb becomes clear.

examples.question: Is it 'Everybody are' or 'Everybody is'?
examples.answer: The correct form is 'Everybody is'. Words like everybody, everyone, somebody, someone, nobody, anybody, each and either are called indefinite pronouns, and they are always singular, even though they seem to refer to many people. So we say 'Everybody is happy', 'Each of the students has a book', and 'Nobody was absent'. A helpful trick: these words often end in '-body' or '-one', and 'one' is clearly singular. In the market you might hear 'Everybody are here', but in writing and in exams it must be 'Everybody is here'. Learn this rule well, because it appears in almost every English paper.

examples.question: What verb do I use with two subjects joined by 'and'?
examples.answer: When two subjects are joined by 'and', they form a plural subject and take a plural verb. For example, 'Bola and Musa are my friends', not 'is my friends'. The two people together make more than one, so the verb must be plural. But watch this special case: when the two joined words refer to a single thing or person, the verb stays singular, as in 'Rice and stew is my favourite meal' (one dish) or 'The head teacher and proprietor was present' (one person holding both roles). So the rule is: 'and' usually makes the subject plural, unless the joined words name one single unit. Read the meaning carefully before choosing the verb.

examples.question: With 'either...or' and 'neither...nor', which subject does the verb agree with?
examples.answer: With 'either...or' and 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject that is NEARER to it, not both. This is called the proximity rule. Look at the noun just before the verb and match the verb to it. Examples: 'Neither the teacher nor the students were ready' — 'students' is nearer, so the verb is plural 'were'. But 'Neither the students nor the teacher was ready' — now 'teacher' is nearer, so the verb is singular 'was'. The same works for 'either...or': 'Either Ada or her brothers are coming.' So before choosing the verb, find the subject closest to it, and let the verb agree with that one. Rearranging the sentence changes the verb.

examples.question: Correct this sentence: The team of players were defeated.

The corrected sentence is: 'The team of players was defeated.' Here is why.

examples.question: Which is correct: 'Ten thousand naira is' or 'are' enough?
examples.answer: The correct form is 'Ten thousand naira is enough.' When an amount of money, a period of time, a distance or a weight is thought of as ONE whole quantity, it takes a singular verb, even though the number sounds plural. So we say 'Ten thousand naira is enough for the books', 'Five years is a long time', and 'Two kilometres is not far to trek.' We treat the whole amount as a single lump, not as separate units. The trick is to ask yourself: is this one total quantity? If yes, use a singular verb. This rule surprises many students because the big number makes them reach for a plural verb, but the meaning is what counts.

examples.question: How do I check concord quickly in an exam?
examples.answer:
Use this quick three-step check on any sentence.

Step 1: find the real subject by asking 'who or what is doing the action?' — and ignore any phrase that comes between the subject and the verb.
Step 2: decide whether that subject is singular or plural, remembering the special cases: everybody/each are singular; 'A and B' is usually plural; with either/or and neither/nor the verb follows the nearer subject; collective nouns and amounts of money or time are usually singular.
Step 3: make the verb agree. A fast test is to strip the sentence to its bare subject and verb, like turning 'The basket of mangoes is heavy' into 'The basket is heavy' — the correct verb becomes obvious.

Practise this and concord errors will disappear.

examples.question: What is tense in English?
examples.answer: Tense is the form of a verb that shows the time of an action, that is, when something happens. There are three main tenses: (1) Present tense - action happening now, e.g. 'I eat'. (2) Past tense - action that has already happened, e.g. 'I ate'. (3) Future tense - action that will happen later, e.g. 'I will eat'. So the verb changes to show whether you are talking about now, before, or later.

examples.question: What is the difference between 'I write' and 'I am writing'?
examples.answer: Both are in the present, but they are different forms. 'I write' is the simple present tense; it shows a habit or something done regularly, e.g. 'I write a letter to my uncle every month.' 'I am writing' is the present continuous tense; it shows an action happening right now, e.g. 'Be quiet, I am writing my note at this moment.' So use the simple present for habits and the present continuous for actions in progress now.

examples.question: Explain the present perfect tense with 'has/have' and when it is used.
examples.answer:
The present perfect tense is formed with 'has' or 'have' plus the past participle of the verb, as in 'She has eaten' or 'They have travelled'. Use 'has' with he, she and it, and 'have' with I, you, we and they. You use it in three main situations.

First, for an action just completed whose result matters now: 'I have finished my homework', so it is ready.
Second, for something that happened at an unstated time in the past: 'I have visited Abuja before.'
Third, for an action that started in the past and still continues: 'She has lived in Kano for ten years.' Words like already, just, ever, never, since and for often signal it. Unlike the simple past, it does not use a finished time word like 'yesterday'.

examples.question: Correct this sentence: She have gone to the market since morning.
examples.answer:
The corrected sentence is: 'She has gone to the market since morning.' Here is the reasoning.

Step 1: identify the subject, 'she', which is third person singular.
Step 2: with he, she or it, the present perfect uses 'has', not 'have'. So 'have gone' must become 'has gone'.
Step 3: notice the word 'since', which is a strong clue that the present perfect tense is correct here, because the action started in the past and continues to now. The full correct sentence is 'She has gone to the market since morning.'

A very common error is using 'have' with a singular subject; always pair he, she and it with 'has'. Keep this in mind and your perfect tenses will be accurate.

examples.question: What is the difference between the simple past and the present perfect?
examples.answer: The simple past and the present perfect both talk about the past, but they are used differently. The SIMPLE PAST describes an action that is finished at a definite past time, usually with a time word: 'I ate rice yesterday', 'We travelled last week.' The PRESENT PERFECT describes an action linked to the present, at an unstated time or with a result now: 'I have eaten rice' (so I am not hungry), 'We have travelled to Jos before.' A key clue: the simple past goes with finished-time words like yesterday, last week and ago, while the present perfect goes with words like already, just, ever, never, since and for. Compare: 'She wrote the letter yesterday' (simple past, definite time) versus 'She has written the letter' (present perfect, done now). Match the tense to whether the time is stated and finished.

examples.question: Change to the past continuous: The children play in the compound.
examples.answer:
The past continuous version is: 'The children were playing in the compound.' Here is how it works.

Step 1: the past continuous is formed with 'was' or 'were' plus a verb ending in -ing.
Step 2: choose 'was' for singular subjects and 'were' for plural ones; since 'children' is plural, we use 'were'.
Step 3: add -ing to the verb, so 'play' becomes 'playing'. This tense describes an action that was going on at some moment in the past, often interrupted by another action, as in 'The children were playing when the rain started.' Compare the three: 'The children play' is a habit, 'The children played' is a finished action, and 'The children were playing' is an action in progress in the past. The continuous form paints the action as ongoing.

examples.question: How do I form the future tense in English?
examples.answer:
There are three common ways to talk about the future.

First, use 'will' or 'shall' plus the base form of the verb, for decisions, promises and predictions: 'I will call you tonight', 'It will rain soon.'
Second, use 'is/am/are going to' plus the base verb, for plans already made or things you can see coming: 'We are going to visit our grandmother next week', 'Look at those clouds, it is going to rain.'
Third, use the present continuous for fixed arrangements with a set time: 'I am travelling to Enugu on Friday.'

Remember that after 'will', the verb never changes: say 'She will come', never 'She will comes' or 'She will came.' Time words like tomorrow, next week and soon usually go with the future tense. Choose the form that matches how sure or how planned the future action is.

examples.question: What are the parts of a formal letter?
examples.answer: A formal letter has these main parts in order: (1) The writer's address and the date, written at the top right. (2) The receiver's address (the address of the person or office you are writing to), written on the left. (3) The salutation or greeting, e.g. 'Dear Sir/Ma'. (4) The title or heading, which states the subject. (5) The body, divided into clear paragraphs. (6) The closing, e.g. 'Yours faithfully'. (7) Your signature and full name. In WAEC, getting these parts and their order right earns important marks.

examples.question: How should I end a formal letter?
examples.answer: How you end a formal letter depends on the salutation you used. If you began with 'Dear Sir' or 'Dear Ma' (because you do not know the person's name), end with 'Yours faithfully'. If you began with the person's name, such as 'Dear Mr Okafor', end with 'Yours sincerely'. After the closing, leave a space for your signature, then write your full name. Remember: only the first word of the closing ('Yours') begins with a capital letter.

examples.question: How is a formal letter different from an informal letter?

examples.question: What are the parts of an informal letter?
examples.answer:
Well done for asking! An informal letter has five main parts.

First, the writer's address at the top right corner, like 'No. 5 Adeola Street, Surulere, Lagos.'

examples.question: What is a synonym?
examples.answer: Great question! A synonym is a word that has the same meaning, or almost the same meaning, as another word. For example, 'big' and 'large' are synonyms, and so are 'happy' and 'glad', 'quick' and 'fast', 'begin' and 'start'. Instead of saying 'The market was big', you can say 'The market was large' and the meaning stays the same. Synonyms make your writing rich and interesting, so you do not repeat the same word again and again. Try finding a synonym for 'small' and use it in a sentence. Well done!

examples.question: What is an antonym?
examples.answer: Good question! An antonym is a word with the opposite meaning of another word. For example, 'hot' is the antonym of 'cold', 'tall' is the antonym of 'short', 'day' is the opposite of 'night', and 'open' is the opposite of 'close'. If Emeka is tall and Chidi is short, the two words paint opposite pictures. Antonyms help us compare and describe things clearly. examples.question: What are homonyms?
examples.answer: Lovely question! Homonyms are words that sound the same or are spelt the same but have different meanings. Think of 'bank': it can mean the place where we keep money, or the side of a river. 'Bat' can be the animal that flies at night, or the wooden bat used in a game. Words that sound alike but are spelt differently, like 'sun' and 'son' or 'flour' and 'flower', are also studied here; we often call them homophones. The sentence around the word tells you which meaning is meant. English is full of these fun twins!

examples.question: Why should I learn synonyms and antonyms?
examples.answer: Wonderful question! Learning synonyms and antonyms makes you a better speaker, writer and reader. Synonyms stop your compositions from repeating one word too many times; instead of writing 'nice' five times, you can use 'lovely', 'pleasant' or 'beautiful'. Antonyms help you describe differences clearly, like a busy Lagos street and a quiet village road. They also help in comprehension tests and Common Entrance examinations, where you are often asked for a word that is nearest or opposite in meaning. Learn a few new words every week and your English will shine!

examples.question: What is a tag question?
examples.answer: Great question! A tag question is a short question we add to the end of a sentence to check or confirm something. For example: 'You are in Primary 4, aren't you?' The first part is a statement, and the little question at the end is the tag. We use tag questions all the time when we speak: 'It is hot today, isn't it?' 'Bola can sing, can't she?' The tag invites the other person to agree or answer. Listen out for tag questions when people around you talk. You will hear them everywhere!

examples.question: What is the rule for forming tag questions?
examples.answer: Well done for asking! The main rule is simple: a positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag. For example: 'Ngozi is your friend, isn't she?' The statement is positive, so the tag 'isn't she' is negative. But 'Ngozi is not here, is she?' has a negative statement, so the tag 'is she' is positive. The tag also uses the same helping verb as the sentence, and a pronoun like he, she, it or they. Think of it like a see-saw: when one side goes up, the other goes down!
examples.system: You are Martha, the SkoolBox AI tutor for Primary 4 students in Nigeria. You follow the NERDC English Studies curriculum for Basic 4. Use very simple words, short sentences, and relatable examples. Always encourage the student.

examples.question: What is the tag question for 'You can swim'?
examples.answer: Let us work it out! The sentence 'You can swim' is positive, so the tag must be negative. The helping verb is 'can', so the tag uses 'can't'. The pronoun stays 'you'. Putting it together: 'You can swim, can't you?' Notice the comma before the tag and the question mark at the end. Here are similar ones: 'Tunde can draw, can't he?' and 'They can dance, can't they?' The pattern is always the same: repeat the helping verb, flip it, add the pronoun. Try making one with 'She can cook.' Excellent work!

examples.question: How do I make a tag question when the sentence has no helping verb, like 'Ada likes rice'?
examples.answer: Very good question! When a sentence has no helping verb, we borrow 'do', 'does' or 'did' for the tag. 'Ada likes rice' is present tense with 'she', so we use 'doesn't': 'Ada likes rice, doesn't she?' For 'They play football', we say: 'They play football, don't they?' For the past tense, 'Musa went to Abuja', we use 'didn't': 'Musa went to Abuja, didn't he?' So do, does and did are helpers we call on when no other helping verb is in the sentence. examples.question: What is the tag question for 'It is not raining'?

examples.question: Why do we use tag questions when we speak?
examples.answer:
Lovely question! We use tag questions for three main reasons.

First, to confirm something we think is true: 'The test is on Monday, isn't it?'
Second, to invite someone to agree with us: 'The jollof rice is delicious, isn't it?'
Third, to start a friendly conversation politely: 'You are new in this school, aren't you?' Tag questions make our speech warm and polite instead of blunt. Nigerians use them every day in the market, at home and in school. Use one politely today and see how friendly it sounds!

examples.question: Complete this sentence with the correct tag: 'Your parents will come to the open day, ...?'
examples.answer: Let us solve it together! The statement 'Your parents will come to the open day' is positive, so the tag must be negative. The helping verb is 'will', and its negative is 'won't'. 'Your parents' becomes the pronoun 'they'. So the full sentence is: 'Your parents will come to the open day, won't they?' Remember the three steps: find the helping verb, flip positive to negative, and change the subject to a pronoun. Try this one yourself: 'Amina will win the prize, ...?' examples.question: Is 'isn't it' correct for every sentence, like some people say?
examples.answer: What a sharp observation! No, 'isn't it' does not fit every sentence, even though we often hear people use it that way. The tag must match the helping verb and the subject of the sentence. We say 'She is tall, isn't she?' but 'They are tall, aren't they?' and 'He can drive, can't he?' Using 'isn't it' everywhere, like 'They have gone, isn't it?', is a common error; the correct tag is 'haven't they?' Now you know the rule, you can speak better English than many adults. examples.question: What is a tense in English?
examples.answer: Great question! A tense tells us when an action happens. There are three main tenses. The present tense is for what happens now or every day: 'Amina eats rice.' The past tense is for what already happened: 'Amina ate rice yesterday.' The future tense is for what will happen later: 'Amina will eat rice tomorrow.' See how the verb 'eat' changes to 'ate' and 'will eat'? The verb carries the time of the action. Listen for tenses when people speak at home and school. You are doing very well!

examples.question: How do I form the past tense of a verb?
examples.answer: Well done for asking! For most verbs, we add -ed to form the past tense: walk becomes walked, play becomes played, and jump becomes jumped. So we say, 'Yesterday, Chidi walked to school.' But some verbs are special and change completely; we call them irregular verbs. Go becomes went, eat becomes ate, see becomes saw, and come becomes came. There is no -ed for these, so we must learn them by heart. Practise by telling a friend three things you did yesterday. Keep it up, you are learning fast!

examples.question: How do I talk about the future in English?
examples.answer: Good question! To talk about the future, we use 'will' or 'shall' before the verb, or 'is going to'. For example: 'I will visit my grandmother in the village next week.' 'We shall write a test on Friday.' 'Ngozi is going to wash the plates after dinner.' Notice that the main verb does not change; 'will' does the work of showing future time. Words like tomorrow, next week and later often appear with the future tense. Try saying three things you will do this weekend. Excellent effort!

examples.question: What is the difference between 'go', 'goes', 'went' and 'will go'?
examples.answer: Lovely question! All four come from the same verb, 'go', but they show different times and persons. We say 'I go to school' and 'they go to school', but 'she goes to school', because with he, she or it we add -es in the present tense. 'Went' is the past tense: 'Emeka went to Kano last month.' 'Will go' is the future: 'Emeka will go to Kano next month.' So the time of the action and the person doing it decide which form to use. Make your own sentences with each form. Well done!

examples.question: Is this sentence correct: 'Yesterday I eat beans'?
examples.answer: Good try, but the sentence is not correct. The word 'yesterday' tells us the action already happened, so we need the past tense of 'eat', which is 'ate'. The correct sentence is: 'Yesterday I ate beans.' Remember, 'eat' is an irregular verb, so we do not say 'eated'. Here are more examples: 'Yesterday I ate rice and stew,' and 'Last week we ate moi-moi at the party.' Always match the time word with the verb form. You spotted a common mistake many pupils make, so well done for checking!

examples.question: What is the present continuous tense?
examples.answer: Great question! The present continuous tense describes an action happening right now, at this very moment. We form it with 'is', 'am' or 'are' plus a verb ending in -ing. For example: 'I am reading my book.' 'Mama is cooking jollof rice.' 'The pupils are singing the national anthem.' Compare it with the simple present: 'Mama cooks every day' talks about a habit, but 'Mama is cooking now' talks about this moment. Look around you and say what people are doing right now using -ing verbs. You are improving every day!

examples.question: Can you give me examples of irregular verbs and their past tense?
examples.answer: Of course! Irregular verbs change completely in the past tense instead of adding -ed. Here are common ones: go becomes went, eat becomes ate, see becomes saw, come becomes came, take becomes took, give becomes gave, run becomes ran, sing becomes sang, write becomes wrote, and buy becomes bought. For example: 'Halima bought bananas at Mile 12 market,' and 'The choir sang beautifully on Sunday.' The best way to learn them is to use them in your own sentences every day. Pick five today and make a sentence with each. Keep practising!

examples.question: Rewrite this sentence in the future tense: 'Ada visits her aunty in Enugu.'

examples.question: What is punctuation?
examples.answer: Punctuation means the special marks we use in writing to make our meaning clear. Examples are the full stop (.), comma (,), question mark (?) and exclamation mark (!). They tell the reader when to pause or stop, and whether we are asking or shouting. Well done!

examples.question: When do we use a question mark?
examples.answer: We use a question mark (?) at the end of a sentence that asks a question. For example: 'What is your name?' and 'Where do you live?' both end with a question mark. If the sentence is not a question, we use a full stop instead. Great job!

examples.question: How do I answer comprehension questions well?
examples.answer: Comprehension means understanding what you read. Follow these steps: (1) Read the whole passage slowly, at least twice. (2) Read each question carefully. (3) Go back to the passage and find the part that answers the question. (4) Answer in a complete sentence, using your own words where you can. Always make sure your answer matches what the passage actually says. Well done!

examples.question: What is concord in English?
examples.answer: Concord (also called agreement) is the grammatical rule that a verb must agree with its subject in number and person. A singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. For example: 'The boy writes well' (singular subject, singular verb) but 'The boys write well' (plural subject, plural verb). Concord is a frequent WAEC area, so always identify the true subject first, then match the verb to it.

examples.question: Choose the correct verb: Each of the students (has/have) a textbook.
examples.answer: The correct answer is 'has': 'Each of the students has a textbook.' Here is the reasoning. The subject is 'Each', not 'students'. Words like each, every, either, neither, everyone and somebody are singular, so they take a singular verb. The phrase 'of the students' is just a modifier and does not change the subject. This is the 'proximity trap' WAEC loves: do not be misled by the plural noun closest to the verb; match the verb to the real subject, which is the singular 'Each'.

examples.question: Why is 'The team are winning' sometimes correct?
examples.answer: This involves a special type called notional concord, which deals with collective nouns such as team, family, government, committee and class. When the group acts as a single unit, use a singular verb: 'The team is winning' (the team as one body). When you are thinking of the individual members acting separately, a plural verb is acceptable: 'The team are arguing among themselves' (the players as individuals). So 'The team are winning' is only correct if you mean the individual players; in most WAEC contexts, treating the collective noun as one unit with a singular verb is the safer choice.

examples.question: What is summary writing?
examples.answer: Summary writing is the skill of reducing a passage to its main points in fewer words, while keeping the original meaning. In WAEC, you are given a passage and asked specific questions, such as 'In three sentences, state the writer's reasons for...'. You must find only the points that answer the question, then express them clearly in your own words. A good summary is brief, accurate, and contains no examples, repetition or personal opinion.

examples.question: Give me steps for answering a summary question in WAEC.
examples.answer: Follow these steps: (1) Read the passage carefully to understand the general idea. (2) Read the summary question and underline exactly what is asked. (3) Read the passage again, picking out only the points that answer that question. (4) Write each point in your own words, in complete sentences. (5) Keep to the number of sentences asked for, and do not add examples, illustrations or your own opinion. (6) Check your spelling and grammar, because expression also carries marks. Always answer only what is asked, no more.

examples.question: Why do students lose marks in summary?
examples.answer: Students commonly lose marks in summary for these reasons: (1) Lifting, that is, copying whole sentences word for word from the passage instead of using their own words. (2) Including points that do not answer the question. (3) Adding examples, repetition or personal opinion. (4) Writing more sentences than required. (5) Poor expression, with grammatical and spelling errors. To score well, answer only the question asked, be brief, use your own words, and write clearly.

examples.question: What are the types of essay tested in WAEC?
examples.answer: WAEC commonly tests these essay types: (1) Narrative - telling a story or describing an event. (2) Descriptive - describing a person, place or thing vividly. (3) Expository - explaining or giving information about a topic. (4) Argumentative - giving reasons for and against a point and taking a stand. (5) Letters (formal and informal) and (6) Article/speech writing. Each type has its own format and tone, so you must first identify the type before you start writing.

examples.question: What is the structure of a good essay?
examples.answer: A good essay has three main parts: (1) Introduction - one paragraph that introduces the topic and catches the reader's interest. (2) Body - several paragraphs, each developing one main point with explanation and examples; ideas should flow logically with linking words. (3) Conclusion - a final paragraph that sums up your points or restates your stand without introducing new ideas. Plan your points before writing, use clear paragraphs, and keep to the topic throughout. Marks are also given for correct grammar, spelling and expression.

examples.question: How do I write a strong argumentative essay?
examples.answer: For an argumentative essay, follow these steps: (1) Take a clear stand, for or against the motion, and state it in your introduction. (2) In the body, give strong, well-reasoned points that support your stand, each with explanation and evidence. (3) Mention one or two opposing points and politely show why your view is stronger; this shows balanced thinking. (4) Use linking expressions such as 'furthermore', 'on the contrary' and 'in addition'. (5) End with a firm conclusion that restates your position. If it is for a debate, remember the features: greeting the audience, the vocative, and an appropriate closing. Be persuasive but polite.

examples.question: Why do we use letters in mathematics?
examples.answer:
We use letters to stand for numbers we do not yet know, or numbers that can change. A letter used this way is called a VARIABLE, and working with them is called algebra. There are two main reasons.

First, to represent an UNKNOWN we want to find: if a book costs an unknown amount, call it x, then 3 books cost 3x, and if you paid 900 naira you can write 3x = 900 and solve for x.
Second, to state a GENERAL rule that works for every number: the area of any rectangle is A = l × w, whatever the actual measurements. Letters make mathematics powerful because one short statement covers infinitely many cases. Any letter works, though x, y, n and a are the most common.

examples.question: What does 5x actually mean?
examples.answer: 5x means 5 MULTIPLIED BY x — in algebra we leave out the multiplication sign to avoid confusing × with the letter x. So if x = 3, then 5x = 5 × 3 = 15. The 5 is called the COEFFICIENT and x is the variable. Be careful with these common misreadings: 5x does NOT mean 'fifty-something' and it does not mean 5 + x. Related notations to know: x on its own means 1x (the coefficient 1 is understood); x² means x × x, not 2x; and xy means x × y. A real-life reading: if a sachet of pure water costs x naira, then 5x is the cost of 5 sachets. Getting comfortable with this shorthand is the first step into algebra.

examples.question: If y = 4, find the value of 3y + 7
examples.answer:
This is substitution — replacing the letter with the number it stands for.

Step 1: write out the expression: 3y + 7.
Step 2: replace y with 4, using brackets for clarity: 3(4) + 7.
Step 3: follow BODMAS and multiply before adding: 3 × 4 = 12.
Step 4: complete the addition: 12 + 7 = 19.

So when y = 4, the value of 3y + 7 is 19. A very common mistake is adding first (4 + 7 = 11, then × 3 = 33), which is wrong — multiplication always comes before addition. Practise with the same expression for other values: when y = 0 the answer is 7, and when y = 10 it is 37.

examples.question: Simplify 7a + 2b - 3a + 5b
examples.answer:
We can only combine LIKE terms — terms with exactly the same letter.

Step 1: group the a terms: 7a and -3a.
Step 2: group the b terms: +2b and +5b.
Step 3: combine each group separately. For a: 7a - 3a = 4a. For b: 2b + 5b = 7b.
Step 4: write the simplified expression: 4a + 7b. We stop here because 4a and 7b are unlike terms and cannot be merged — a common error is writing 11ab, which is wrong. Think of a as agbalumo and b as banana: 4 agbalumo and 7 bananas stay separate; you cannot call them 11 of one fruit. Tip: when regrouping, always carry each term's sign along with it.

examples.question: Write an expression for: a number multiplied by 4, then decreased by 9
examples.answer:
Let us translate the words step by step.

Step 1: choose a letter for 'a number' — let us use n.
Step 2: 'multiplied by 4' gives 4n.
Step 3: 'decreased by 9' means subtract 9, giving 4n - 9.

So the expression is 4n - 9. Order matters here: 4n - 9 is not the same as 9 - 4n, and it is not 4(n - 9), which would mean the subtraction happened first. Useful vocabulary for these questions: 'increased by' or 'more than' means add; 'decreased by', 'less than' or 'reduced by' means subtract; 'product' or 'times' means multiply; 'quotient' or 'shared' means divide. Reading the words slowly, in order, is the whole skill.

examples.question: Solve the simple equation x + 8 = 15
examples.answer:
An equation is a statement that two things are equal, and solving means finding the value of the letter that makes it true. The golden rule: whatever you do to one side, do to the other, so the balance is kept.

Step 1: we want x alone, but 8 is added to it.
Step 2: undo the addition by subtracting 8 from BOTH sides: x + 8 - 8 = 15 - 8.
Step 3: simplify: x = 7.
Step 4: always check by substituting back into the original: 7 + 8 = 15. Correct! Picture a weighing scale with x and 8 on one pan balancing 15 on the other: remove 8 from one pan and you must remove 8 from the other, or it tips. That balance idea carries you through all of algebra.

examples.question: Solve 6x = 42
examples.answer:
Here x is being MULTIPLIED by 6, so we undo it with the opposite operation, division.

Step 1: identify what is holding x: the coefficient 6.
Step 2: divide both sides by 6: 6x ÷ 6 = 42 ÷ 6.
Step 3: on the left the 6s cancel, leaving x; on the right 42 ÷ 6 = 7. So x = 7.
Step 4: check by substituting: 6 × 7 = 42. Correct! A real-life version: if 6 identical exercise books cost 42 naira altogether, then each book costs 7 naira.

Remember the pairing of opposite operations: addition undoes subtraction, subtraction undoes addition, multiplication undoes division, and division undoes multiplication.

examples.question: Aisha has some oranges. Her mother gives her 12 more and she now has 30. Form an equation and find how many she had at first.
examples.answer:
Let us turn the story into algebra.

Step 1: let the unknown starting number of oranges be n.
Step 2: her mother gives 12 more, so she now has n + 12.
Step 3: the story says this equals 30, so the equation is n + 12 = 30.
Step 4: solve by subtracting 12 from both sides: n = 30 - 12 = 18. So Aisha had 18 oranges at first.
Step 5: check against the story — 18 oranges plus 12 more gives 30. Correct! This four-part method works for every word problem: name the unknown with a letter, translate each sentence into symbols, solve the equation, then check the answer makes sense in the original story.

examples.question: What is a fraction and what do the two numbers mean?
examples.answer: A fraction represents part of a whole. It is written with two numbers separated by a line, as in 3/4. The bottom number is the DENOMINATOR: it tells you how many equal parts the whole has been divided into. The top number is the NUMERATOR: it tells you how many of those parts you are talking about. So in 3/4, the whole was cut into 4 equal parts and we are considering 3 of them. Picture a loaf of agege bread cut into 4 equal pieces: if you take 3, you have taken 3/4 of the loaf. The parts must be EQUAL for the fraction to be meaningful — cutting a loaf into 4 uneven pieces and taking one is not truly one quarter.

examples.question: What are equivalent fractions?
examples.answer: Equivalent fractions are different fractions that represent the SAME amount. For example, 1/2, 2/4, 3/6 and 5/10 are all equivalent — each is half of the whole. You create them by multiplying (or dividing) the numerator AND denominator by the same number: starting from 1/2, multiply both by 3 to get 3/6; multiply both by 5 to get 5/10. The value does not change because you have cut the whole into more pieces but taken proportionally more of them. Picture two identical oranges: cut one into 2 parts and take 1, cut the other into 4 parts and take 2 — you are holding the same quantity of orange. This idea is the basis for simplifying fractions and for adding fractions with different denominators.

examples.question: Simplify 18/24 to its lowest terms.
examples.answer:
Simplifying (or reducing) means dividing the numerator and denominator by their HCF until no common factor remains.

Step 1: find the HCF of 18 and 24. The factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18; the factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. The highest common one is 6.
Step 2: divide both parts by 6: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4. So 18/24 = 3/4.
Step 3: check that 3 and 4 share no factor other than 1 — correct, so this is fully simplified. If you cannot spot the HCF at once, divide by any common factor repeatedly: 18/24 ÷ 2 = 9/12, then ÷ 3 = 3/4. You reach the same answer, just in more steps.

examples.question: Add 2/5 + 1/3
examples.answer:
To add fractions the denominators must be the SAME, so we first find a common denominator.

Step 1: find the LCM of 5 and 3, which is 15.
Step 2: convert each fraction to fifteenths. For 2/5, multiply top and bottom by 3: 2/5 = 6/15. For 1/3, multiply top and bottom by 5: 1/3 = 5/15.
Step 3: now that the denominators match, add the numerators only: 6/15 + 5/15 = 11/15.
Step 4: check whether it simplifies — 11 is prime and does not divide 15, so 11/15 is the final answer. The rule to remember: never add the denominators. You are counting pieces of the same size, so only the count (numerator) increases.

examples.question: How do I multiply fractions, like 2/3 × 3/4?
examples.answer:
Multiplying fractions is simpler than adding — no common denominator needed. Just multiply straight across.

Step 1: multiply the numerators: 2 × 3 = 6.
Step 2: multiply the denominators: 3 × 4 = 12.
Step 3: that gives 6/12, which simplifies by dividing both by 6 to give 1/2.

So 2/3 × 3/4 = 1/2. Tip: you can cancel BEFORE multiplying to keep numbers small — the 3 on top and the 3 below cancel, leaving 2/1 × 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2, the same answer with easier arithmetic. What does it mean? The word 'of' signals multiplication: 2/3 × 3/4 asks for two-thirds OF three-quarters. If three-quarters of a bag of rice remains and you use two-thirds of it, you used half the original bag.

examples.question: Why do we turn the second fraction upside down when dividing, like 1/2 ÷ 1/4?
examples.answer: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its RECIPROCAL (the fraction turned upside down). So 1/2 ÷ 1/4 becomes 1/2 × 4/1 = 4/2 = 2. Why does this work? Division asks 'how many of these fit into that?' So 1/2 ÷ 1/4 asks: how many quarters fit into one half? Picture half a loaf of bread and quarter-loaf pieces — exactly 2 quarters fit into a half. The answer 2 matches, so the rule is sound, not magic. Another example: 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 3/4 × 8/1 = 24/4 = 6, meaning six eighths fit into three quarters. Notice that dividing by a fraction smaller than 1 gives a BIGGER answer, which surprises students until they picture the pieces.

examples.question: Convert the improper fraction 17/5 to a mixed number, and 2 3/4 to an improper fraction.
examples.answer: An IMPROPER fraction has a numerator larger than its denominator; a MIXED number combines a whole number with a proper fraction. FIRST, 17/5 to a mixed number: divide 17 by 5, which gives 3 remainder 2. The quotient 3 becomes the whole number, the remainder 2 becomes the new numerator, and the denominator stays 5. So 17/5 = 3 2/5. SECOND, 2 3/4 to an improper fraction: multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator: (2 × 4) + 3 = 11, keeping the denominator 4. So 2 3/4 = 11/4. Check by reversing: 11 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 3, giving back 2 3/4. Correct! Picture 2 3/4 loaves of bread: each whole loaf is 4 quarters, so 2 loaves are 8 quarters, plus 3 more makes 11 quarters.

examples.question: Musa spent 2/5 of his 2,000 naira pocket money on books. How much did he spend and how much is left?
examples.answer:
The word 'of' tells us to multiply.

Step 1: find 2/5 of 2,000. Divide by the denominator first: 2,000 ÷ 5 = 400, so one fifth is 400 naira.
Step 2: multiply by the numerator: 400 × 2 = 800. So Musa spent 800 naira on books.
Step 3: find what is left by subtracting: 2,000 - 800 = 1,200 naira remaining. Alternative check: if he spent 2/5, he has 3/5 left, and 3 × 400 = 1,200 naira — the same answer, which confirms our working. This 'divide by the bottom, multiply by the top' method works for finding any fraction of any quantity, and you will use it constantly for discounts, shares and percentages.

examples.question: What is the difference between perimeter and area?
examples.answer: PERIMETER is the total distance AROUND the outside of a shape — a length, measured in cm, m or km. AREA is the amount of SURFACE the shape covers — measured in square units like cm² or m². Picture a football field: the perimeter is how far you run if you jog once round the touchlines; the area is how much grass is needed to cover it. For a rectangle 8 m long and 5 m wide: perimeter = 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 m, while area = 8 × 5 = 40 m². Notice perimeter comes from ADDING sides and keeps ordinary units, while area comes from MULTIPLYING and takes square units. Losing that 'squared' in an exam answer costs marks, so always write the unit carefully.

examples.question: Find the area and perimeter of a rectangle 12 cm long and 7 cm wide.
examples.answer:
Let us use the two formulas. AREA = length × width.

Step 1: substitute the values: 12 × 7.
Step 2: multiply: 84. So the area is 84 cm² (square centimetres). PERIMETER = 2 × (length + width).
Step 1: add length and width: 12 + 7 = 19.
Step 2: multiply by 2, because there are two lengths and two widths: 19 × 2 = 38.

So the perimeter is 38 cm. You could also add all four sides: 12 + 7 + 12 + 7 = 38 cm, which confirms the answer. Note the units carefully: area is in cm² because we multiplied two lengths, while perimeter stays in cm because we only added lengths.

examples.question: How do I find the area of a triangle?
examples.answer:
The formula is: Area = 1/2 × base × height. The BASE is any side you choose, and the HEIGHT is the perpendicular distance from that base up to the opposite corner — it must meet the base at a right angle, and it is not necessarily one of the sides. Example: a triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm.

Step 1: multiply base by height: 10 × 6 = 60.
Step 2: take half: 60 ÷ 2 = 30.

So the area is 30 cm². Why the half? Because any triangle is exactly half of a rectangle with the same base and height — draw a rectangle, cut along its diagonal, and you get two identical triangles. Forgetting to halve is the most common mistake in this topic.

examples.question: What are the parts of a circle?
examples.answer: A circle has several named parts. The CENTRE is the fixed middle point. The RADIUS is the distance from the centre to any point on the circle. The DIAMETER is the distance right across the circle through the centre, and it is always twice the radius (d = 2r). The CIRCUMFERENCE is the distance all the way around — the circle's version of perimeter. A CHORD is any straight line joining two points on the circle (the diameter is the longest chord). An ARC is a part of the circumference, and a SECTOR is a slice bounded by two radii and an arc, shaped like a piece of cut watermelon. Everyday circles: a car tyre, the top of a milk tin, and the round tray used for selling groundnuts.
